subject: mathematics_2b
question_text: Give the solution of x sin²(y/x)dx = ydx − xdy, which passes through the point (1, π/4).

mark_split.label: Apply the given point and finish

insider_note: The equation is printed with dx and dy mixed on both sides, so the very first mark is for correctly isolating dy/dx = … before anything else — a sign error at this rearranging step invalidates every later line.

steps.label: Rearrange and substitute
steps.margin_note: Two marks. Collect both dy terms on one side and both dx terms on the other, then divide, before checking homogeneity.
steps.memory_tip: Move xdy to the left with x sin²(y/x)dx, and ydx to the right on its own, so dy/dx isolates cleanly.
lines: The given D.E is x sin²(y/x)dx = ydx − xdy
Put y = vx ⇒ dy/dx = v + x·dv/dx
steps.why: The equation is given with dx and dy mixed, so it must first be rearranged into the standard dy/dx = … form; once written that way, the right side depends only on y/x, confirming it is homogeneous and ready for y = vx.
common_mistakes: Losing the minus sign when moving x sin²(y/x)dx across the equals sign.
Dividing by dx incorrectly and leaving dy/dx = y − x sin²(y/x) without the /x on the first term.

steps.label: Separate the variables
steps.margin_note: One mark. The two v terms cancel, leaving only −sin²v on the right.
steps.memory_tip: Whenever the plain v cancels between both sides, what remains is always the part that came from differentiating v.
steps.why: The two v terms cancel exactly, and dividing both sides by −sin²v and taking the reciprocal turns the equation into −cosec²v dv = dx/x, separated into v-terms and x-terms.
common_mistakes: Missing the v cancellation and carrying an extra term forward.
Writing 1/sin²v as sin²v instead of cosec²v.

steps.label: Integrate both sides
steps.margin_note: Two marks. ∫cosec²v dv = −cot v, so the two minus signs together give a plain cot v on the left.
steps.memory_tip: cosec²v integrates to −cot v — the leading minus sign in −cosec²v then flips it back to +cot v.
steps.why: cosec²v is the derivative of −cot v, so ∫cosec²v dv = −cot v; with the leading minus sign on the left already in the equation, the two signs cancel and leave a positive cot v.
common_mistakes: Losing track of the two minus signs and writing −cot v = log x + c instead of cot v = log x + c.

steps.label: Return to x and y
steps.margin_note: One mark. Substitute v = y/x directly — no rearranging is needed first, since cot v is already isolated.
steps.memory_tip: cot v = log x + c is already the general family in v — just replace v by y/x.
lines: Put v = y/x: cot(y/x) = log x + c
steps.why: With cot v already isolated on one side, the substitution v = y/x carries directly into the family of solutions, giving the general relation in the original variables x and y.
common_mistakes: Writing cot(x/y) instead of cot(y/x), inverting the ratio.
Re-deriving the equation instead of simply substituting into (2).

steps.label: Apply the given point and finish
steps.margin_note: The last mark. Substitute x = 1, y = π/4 to find c, then state the final particular solution.
steps.memory_tip: log 1 = 0 and cot(π/4) = 1 — both simplify away instantly at this point.
lines: If (x, y) = (1, π/4) lies on this curve, then
steps.why: Substituting the given point into the general family (2) fixes the constant c, and putting that value back gives the one curve through (1, π/4) that the question asks for.
common_mistakes: Substituting the point into the un-integrated equation (1) instead of the family (2).
Writing the final answer with log|x| when the working already used log x for a positive x = 1 point, which is consistent but should not be swapped mid-answer.
